questions.question: A bag has 8 red balls and 2 blue balls. You pick one ball. What is more likely?
questions.explain: There are 8 red and only 2 blue, so red has more chances to be picked. The trap is to think two colours always means the same chance.

questions.question: A jar has 5 green beads and 5 yellow beads. You pick one bead. What do you expect?
questions.explain: 5 green and 5 yellow are the same number, so neither colour has an edge. The trap is to pick one colour as more likely when the counts match.

questions.question: A box has 3 pencils and 10 erasers. You reach in with your eyes closed. What is less likely to come out?
questions.explain: There are only 3 pencils but 10 erasers, so a pencil is less likely to come out. The trap is to swap which one is more or less likely.

questions.question: A hat has 6 white socks and 2 black socks. You grab one sock in the dark. What is more likely?
questions.explain: 6 white socks and 2 black socks means white has more chances to be grabbed. The trap is to say the colour with fewer socks is more likely.

questions.question: Your bag has 7 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. You close your eyes and pick one. What is more likely?
questions.explain: 7 red and 3 blue means red has more chances to be picked. The trap is to think two colours always means the same chance.

questions.question: You have a spinner with 4 red parts and 2 blue parts. You spin it many times. What do you expect?
questions.explain: 4 red parts and 2 blue parts means red covers more of the spinner, so it lands more often. The trap is to say the smaller colour is more likely.

questions.question: Your pencil case has 12 stickers and 4 erasers. You reach in with your eyes closed. What is more likely to come out?
questions.explain: 12 stickers and 4 erasers means stickers have more chances to come out first. The trap is to swap which item is more likely.

questions.question: A bag has 6 red balls, 2 blue balls, and 2 green balls. You pick one ball. Compare getting red to getting green.
questions.explain: 6 red and 2 green means red has more chances to be picked. The trap is to think that because there are three colours, all are the same.

questions.question: A spinner has 3 equal parts: red, blue, and green. You spin once. Is red more likely than blue?
questions.explain: The three parts are equal, so red and blue each take up the same amount of the spinner. The trap is to think one colour is more likely just because it is listed first.

questions.question: A bag has 4 red balls and 4 blue balls. You add 3 more red balls. Now compare getting red to getting blue.
questions.explain: After adding 3 red, there are 7 red and 4 blue, so red is now more likely. The trap is to forget the added balls and say they are still the same.

questions.question: Maya's bin has 9 blue cubes and 3 red cubes. She takes one cube without looking. Which colour is more likely?
questions.explain: There are 9 blue cubes and only 3 red cubes, so blue is more likely. More of a colour means a better chance, not the same chance.

questions.question: Ben spins a spinner at the school fair. It has 5 equal yellow parts and 1 green part. Which colour is less likely?
questions.explain: Only 1 part is green and 5 parts are yellow, so green is less likely. Fewer parts means a smaller chance.

questions.question: Ms. Lee wants a bag where picking red and picking blue are equally likely. Which bag should she use?
questions.explain: Equally likely means the same number of each colour, so 5 red and 5 blue works. A bag with 9 red and 3 blue is not equal, even though both colours are inside.

questions.question: Nina has a bag of marbles. She wants to know if green or purple is more likely to be picked. What should she do first?
questions.explain: First count how many of each colour are in the bag. The colour with more marbles is more likely, so you cannot just say the two are equal.

questions.question: A jar has 8 green cubes and 3 orange cubes. Sara takes out 6 green cubes. Now she picks one cube without looking. Which colour is more likely?
questions.explain: After 6 green cubes are taken out, 2 green and 3 orange are left, so orange is more likely. Use the cubes left in the jar, not the first counts.

questions.question: Tom's bag has 6 yellow balls and no black balls. He wants yellow and black to be equally likely. How many black balls should he add?
questions.explain: Equally likely means the same number of each, so he adds 6 black balls to match the 6 yellow balls. Adding none keeps yellow certain, not equal.

questions.question: A spinner has 8 equal parts. 3 parts are red, 3 parts are blue, and 2 parts are green. Kai spins it once. Which sentence is true?
questions.explain: Red has 3 parts and blue has 3 parts, so red and blue are equally likely. Green has only 2 parts, so green is the least likely, not the most.

questions.question: A bag has 7 white buttons and 2 black buttons. Jonas picks one button without looking. He says white and black are equally likely. Which sentence is right?
options: He is right, because both colours are in the bag.
He is wrong, because white has more buttons.
He is wrong, because black has the better chance.
He is wrong, because white is impossible to pick.
questions.explain: There are 7 white buttons and only 2 black, so white is more likely, not the same. Having both colours in the bag does not make them equally likely.
